analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states and cities that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in July 2025 and sent to the Banking Committee, where it has received no further action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a federal fund with $100 million a year for five years. States, cities, and tribal governments that pass a law guaranteeing free, full legal representation to low-income tenants facing eviction or loss of a housing subsidy can apply for grants. Federal money would go first to places that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental help.
analysis.who_benefits: Tenants with incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty line who are facing eviction or termination of a housing subsidy. They would get a lawyer at no cost. Studies of similar local laws consistently find that tenants with counsel are far more likely to stay in their homes. States and cities that adopt the right to counsel also gain federal money to help pay for it.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 in grants to state, local, and tribal governments [S2].
Covered tenants are those at or below 200% of the federal poverty line facing an eviction action or a termination of a housing subsidy, and representation must be full and free of charge [S2].

Federal grants are prioritized for jurisdictions that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' written notice before eviction, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance [S2].
Grant money can pay the actual costs of the right to counsel, including training and recruiting attorneys to represent tenants [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through $500 million in new spending over five years. Landlords would also face a change in the courtroom balance: tenants with lawyers are harder to evict, and eviction cases would take longer and cost more to pursue. States that want the grants would need to fund the program locally and could be nudged toward passing eviction restrictions to win priority funding.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $500 million over five years in new federal spending without a corresponding funding source or offset [S2].
A lawyer protects a tenant's rights in court but does not pay rent that is owed; representation can delay an eviction without solving the underlying arrears [S2].
Priority funding is steered toward jurisdictions that limit no-fault evictions and require 30-day notice, which landlords argue raises their costs and can make them more reluctant to rent [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one-fifth of tenants who face eviction without any lawyer, this is a direct, tangible benefit at a modest federal cost. The strongest objection is that the grant design conditions federal money on state eviction restrictions that landlords bear, and that legal defense does not address the rent arrears driving most evictions. On balance, the benefits to tenants are concrete and the costs are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on July 24, 2025, joined by Senators Van Hollen, Wyden, Sanders, and Blumenthal [S2].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; the bill is simply sitting in committee. Landlords and the status quo are unaffected while it waits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is waiting

for.name: Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought on four original cosponsors [S2].

for.name: Chris Van Hollen, Ron Wyden, Bernie Sanders, and Richard Blumenthal

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no opposition has been recorded; all five sponsors are Democrats or independents, so any partisan split is unknown so far.

industries.note: Tenants with free lawyers win or delay more evictions, so eviction cases cost landlords more time and money. Landlords bear this cost without a direct voice in the bill's drafting.

industries.industry: Civil legal aid providers and tenant-side attorneys
industries.note: The fund pays for training and recruiting lawyers to represent tenants, creating paid legal work that directly serves tenants' interests.
Jurisdictions that pass a right-to-counsel law can win federal grants covering part of the cost, though they must certify they are fiscally responsible for the program.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills introduced by individual members never get a hearing, and this one has been in the Banking Committee with no movement since July 2025 and only five sponsors. Unless a companion House bill and broader support emerge, it is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
